distinct_answers.text: Yes — the distinction is stark. The most intense and damaging hatred in M06-A operates within existing bonds: brothers hating a brother (Joseph's brothers), son hating father's heir (Esau/Jacob), husband withdrawing love from wife (group 550-NEW-01), Amnon's post-violation hatred of Tamar. Hatred within existing relational bonds violates the space where trust and expectation existed, which multiplies the damage.

Contempt operates most destructively within covenant relationships: Israel's contempt of God (their covenantal partner). Between individuals: the comfortable person's contempt of the suffering is more damaging in close relationships (Job 12:5: "in the thought of one who is at ease").
These characteristics operate across all relational distances without significant differentiation in the verse evidence — abhorrence, cruelty, and malice can be directed at those near or far.

Reproach is most damaging when received from those close — Job 19:19: "all my intimate friends abhor me" — the reproach from intimate friends shatters where reproach from strangers might merely sting. Psa 55:12-13: "it is not an enemy who taunts me...but it is you, a man, my equal, my companion" — betrayal by a close associate is qualitatively different.

The cluster's characteristics consistently transcend relational boundaries — they are not restricted to existing bonds but extend toward strangers, enemies, the world. The evidence for universal scope: "do good to everyone" (Gal 6:10 — Group 1098); "kind to the ungrateful and the evil" (Luk 6:35 — Group 1469); "comfort all who mourn" (Isa 61:2 — Group 1742); "God was reconciling the world to himself" (2Cor 5:19 — Group 2069); "show perfect courtesy toward all people" (Tit 3:2 — Groups 1103, 1262). The cluster teaches that these characteristics have a universal relational scope defined by the person's condition of need rather than by pre-existing relational bonds. The community of faith retains priority (Gal 6:10 — Group 1098: "especially to those of the household of faith") but the scope is not restricted to it.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — the cluster contains both bonded (covenant, community) and boundary-crossing examples. Abraham's intercession for Sodom (Gen 18:23–28, VSG M26-A2-015) crosses relational boundaries — he intercedes for a city of strangers. The king who "did justice and righteousness" (Jer 22:15, VSG M26-A2-012) does so in his administrative role — for all within his community. The righteous person's outward-flowing righteousness (Amo 5:24: "like an ever-flowing stream") does not respect relational categories — it flows to whoever is in need.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — the commissioned avenger (Rom 13:4) serves all within the civic jurisdiction, not only those with existing relational bonds. The protection of justice crosses relational distance.

**[CLUSTER — T4.5]** E. Righteousness in M26 operates within existing relational bonds AND crosses relational boundaries. The outward-flowing character of righteousness in A2-012 is not bounded by covenant or community — it reaches toward whoever needs it. However, the covenantal context is the primary context of God's righteousness (A1-003), and the community context is the primary context of the righteous person's social impact (A2-015). Both within-bonds and boundary-crossing modes are present.

VCG06 (self-attributed wisdom): the person who believes themselves wise is closed to receiving from others — wisdom as a self-boundary. VCG07 (wisdom of this age): those whose inner orientation is worldly wisdom are bounded from receiving divine wisdom.
VCG04 (M15-B — judicial withholding): God can withhold understanding as a judicial act — a divine boundary on understanding.
VCG05 (1Sa 2:12): not knowing the Lord as relational boundary marker. VCG09 (Act 17:30): culpable ignorance as boundary between former times and present accountability.
VCG06 (a.rum): the prudent vs fool boundary — discernment as the character-marker that distinguishes.
VCG03: divine counsel as the boundary against which human counsel stands — no counsel can override divine purpose (Isa 14:27).
No boundary dynamics evidenced in M15-F.
No explicit boundary dynamics.
VCG01 (1Cor 1:18): the logos of the cross draws a boundary — those perishing and those being saved differentiated by their reception.
Territorial/jurisdictional boundary in Jude 9, not inner-being boundary dynamics.

The relational-anxiety group (M20-A-NEW-05: 1Sa 9:5; 10:2) shows da.ag operating specifically within a family bond (parent-child). The anxiety is proportional to the relational bond — the father is anxious about the son, not about strangers.

The provocation-discouragement dynamic (athumeō, Col 3:21) operates within the parent-child family bond — the most intimate human relational context. The inflicted discouragement (ka.eh, Eze 13:22) operates in a community-prophetic context — the false prophet's authority within a community makes the disheartening effective.

Both within and across: (1) Within existing bonds: chen group 889-002 (the favour-dynamic within the servant-master or suppliant-benefactor relationship — Gen 18:3; Rut 2:2; Est 5:2). Ba.rakh group 1299-003 (the priestly blessing within Israel's covenantal structure — Num 6:24). (2) Across relational distance: ba.rakh group 1299-001 (Gen 12:3 — "in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed") — the Abrahamic blessing explicitly crosses tribal/national boundaries. Charis group 888-001 (Rom 4:16 — "guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham") — grace crossing the Jew/Gentile boundary.

Primarily within existing social structure: the approval and favour-goodness texts (632-003; 542-001) operate within the person's relational context (community approval, royal approval, family wellbeing). The goodness characteristic does not show the same boundary-crossing pattern as M39-A.

M46-B evidences that hardness operates across relational distance: the rich man's indifference to Lazarus (Luk 16:19-21) is toward someone at his gate — proximate but relationally distant. The failure of pity in 2Sa 12:4 is toward the poor man's lamb — the rich man takes from poverty, having no relational bond with the poor man. Hardness operates toward those outside existing relational bonds — the rich and the poor, the wealthy visitor and the shabby petitioner.

Giving in M46-D crosses relational distance: the Macedonian churches' generosity is toward the Jerusalem believers (2Cor 8:1-4) — a cross-cultural, cross-geographical giving. The giving to the poor commanded in Luk 14:13 specifically names those without existing relational bonds (the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind — those who cannot repay). M46-D's giving is cross-relational-distance giving.

M01-A operates consistently across relational distance — fear of God applies to the person's treatment of strangers (Lev 25:36-37: not exploiting a stranger's poverty), servants (Lev 25:43: no ruthless domination over a servant who is a fellow Israelite), enemies (Deu 25:18: Amalekites' attack on the weak is evidence of absent God-fear), and foreigners (Act 10:35: "anyone who fears God and does what is right is acceptable to him regardless of nationality"). The characteristic operates across all relational distance and difference. It does not narrow to existing bonds.

M01-B's social fear (B-VCG-04) operates across relational difference in the direction of crowd-management: the leaders' fear of the crowd is fear across social distance (the crowd as mass, not individuals in relationship). M01-B's self-preservation fear (B-VCG-05) also operates across relational distance — Jacob's fear of Esau (Gen 32:7-11), the Gibeonites' fear of the covenant community (Jos 9:24).

M01-A's ethical dimension operates specifically in power-asymmetry relationships: Lev 19:14 (the vulnerable deaf and blind), Lev 25:43 (the servant). Fear of God operates precisely where power difference would otherwise enable exploitation. The characteristic does not narrow to relational equals.

M01-A operates consistently across all relational bonds and distances. The characteristic's ethical dimension specifically addresses power-asymmetric relationships where relational exploitation would otherwise be possible. This confirms that fear-of-God is not a parochial characteristic limited to in-group relationships but operates as a universal governing orientation.

Yes, clearly. The covenant-relationship context produces the most intense and sustained anger: God's burning anger against Israel is repeatedly deeper, more persistent, and more personally significant precisely because of the covenant bond that has been violated. Num 32:13 (M02-B-VCG-01): forty years of sustained anger because Israel is God's covenant people who betrayed covenant. Deu 32:21 (M02-E-VCG-02): jealousy stirred by Israel "worshipping a non-god" — the violation is intensified because the devotion was owed covenantally. The covenant bond intensifies the anger when it is violated.

Against foreign nations, the anger operates differently — as a categorical judicial force rather than a covenantally personal one: Isa 34:2 (M02-B-VCG-06): "the Lord's fury is directed against all nations" — this is comprehensive, judicial, and less personally relational than the Israel-specific corpus.

Yes, with clear differences. Within existing relational bonds (M03-A-VCG-01 — bereavement weeping), grief is deep, personal, and often inconsolable — the bond's depth determines the grief's depth (David's grief for Absalom as paradigmatic). Across relational distance (M03-A-VCG-04 — prophetic compassion weeping; M03-A-VCG-05 — commanded weeping-with), grief requires a deliberate act of will and identification: "weep with those who weep" (Rom 12:15) is a command, indicating that cross-relational grief requires volitional engagement rather than arising automatically from bond. In eschatological contexts (M03-A-VCG-05), grief at the loss of Babylon (Rev 18 corpus) is grief arising from investment-bond (merchants who loved Babylon's prosperity) rather than personal relationship.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Exultation within the covenant community is the dominant pattern — the Psalms' exultation is always within the context of Israel's covenant relationship with YHWH. The one exception that crosses relational distance is Exo 18:9 (Jethro, a Midianite priest, rejoices at hearing of God's acts for Israel) — a non-Israelite exulting in YHWH's saving acts for another's people. This suggests exultation can occur across covenantal distance when the object (God's character and acts) transcends covenantal membership.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. Joy within existing bonds is more readily transmitted and completed: the sunchairo passages (M04-D) presuppose existing relational bonds in the community (shepherd's neighbours, body members, Paul and Philippians); 2Jo 12 explicitly argues that the joy of existing fellowship reaches its completeness only in face-to-face meeting — relational distance limits Joy's completeness. Across relational distance: Act 15:3 (Barnabas and Paul bringing joy across geographical distance through news) — Joy can cross relational distance through news-bearing but with less immediate impact. The Johannine emphasis on face-to-face completion (2Jo 12; 3Jo 14) suggests that Joy's fullest relational form requires proximity.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Act 16:34's household-encompassing joy shows the characteristic radiating most immediately through existing relational bonds (family). Luk 1:44 (Spirit-joy communicated across the intimate encounter of kinswomen) confirms existing-bond primacy. Mat 5:12 and 1Pe 4:13 address communities of faith under persecution — existing bonds of shared faith. No evidence of Suffering-Joy operating specifically across relational distance or strangers in this corpus.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The good-news and good-word register (M04-O-VCG-01) can operate across relational distance — Pro 25:25 ("like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country") explicitly affirms that Gladness through good news reaches across geographical distance. The covenantal Gladness (M04-O-VCG-04 — God's promises) is inherently non-proximate — it involves trusting a word not yet fulfilled. The relational-evaluative Gladness (M04-L-VCG-02 — Ruth's love, David's men's goodness) requires existing relational bonds to be evident and assessed.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The relational-delight instances (M04-N; M04-H-VCG-02) are predominantly within existing bonds: Jer 31:20 (God's Delight in Ephraim — the covenantal parent-child bond); 1Sa 19:1 (Jonathan and David — existing friendship bond); Mic 1:16 (parental bond); 1Th 2:8 (Paul and the Thessalonians — apostolic-community bond). The diplomatic-preference idiom (M04-H-VCG-03) operates across hierarchical and political relationships where existing bonds of authority structure the Delight-reference. Psa 73:25 and Psa 37:4's Delight in God operate within the covenantal bond. The evidence suggests Delight is primarily bond-internal: it is sustained and expressed within existing relational contexts rather than extending primarily across relational distance.

**[CHAR-5]** E — M04-J's relational pleasantness is primarily bond-internal: Psa 133:1 (brothers dwelling together), 2Sa 1:26 (the deep friendship of David and Jonathan), Song 1:16; 7:6 (the beloved relationship). The speech-Pleasure (Pro 16:24) can operate across relational distance but is most effective within bonds of mutual respect. The ni.cho.ach worship-Pleasure operates within the covenantal relationship. The cross-boundary instance: Num 15:14 ("if a stranger is sojourning with you… and he wishes to offer a food offering, with a pleasing aroma to the Lord, he shall do as you do") — the worship-Pleasure relationship is extended to include resident foreigners who observe the same ritual conditions.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Wonder operates across both: (1) **Within the covenant community** — the primary VCG-01 context is Israel's internal worship and memory tradition (the Psalms, Chronicles); (2) **Across national boundaries** — 1Ch 16:24; Psa 96:3 ("declare his glory among the nations, his marvellous works among all the peoples") — Wonder extends missionally outward to all peoples; Exo 34:10 ("all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the Lord") — the witness of Wonder is explicitly intended for surrounding nations; (3) **2Ch 26:15** — Uzziah's fame spreading "far" because he was marvellously helped — wonder-acts creating a reputation that extends across geographical distance.

**[CLUSTER]** E — A consistent cluster-level pattern: **all seven operate most fully within existing relational bonds; most can also cross relational distance but with reduced intensity**. Joy (Char 2) is the most carefully documented in this respect: Joh 16:22 and 2Jo 12 confirm that Joy reaches its completeness only in face-to-face proximity; Gladness (Char 3) explicitly confirms cross-distance operation (Pro 25:25 — "good news from a far country" is like cold water to a thirsty soul); Wonder (Char 6) has the widest cross-distance scope — its missional proclamation (1Ch 16:24; Psa 96:3) is explicitly directed across national and cultural boundaries. The exceptions to bond-preference: Wonder and Joy both operate cross-distance more effectively than Delight (Char 4), which is primarily bond-internal (the diplomatic idiom and relational attachment of M04-H-VCG-02 are both within existing relationships). Suffering-Joy (Char 7) shows no evidence of operating specifically across relational distance — it is consistently community-internal.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Within existing covenantal bonds (Israel-God relationship in M07-C; Paul-Corinthians in M07-B-VCG-05; family relationships in M07-B-VCG-03), shame functions as a relational signal — it can be received, corrected, and lead to restored relationship because the bond exists and can bear the weight. Across relational distance (enemies in M07-A, opponents in M07-B-VCG-01), shame is a judicial/moral verdict rather than a relational instrument — it is the exposure and collapse of standing before one who stands against the person, not a call to relational restoration. The community discipline passage (2Th 3:14) is notable: isolation from the disobedient person is prescribed precisely to signal the relational rupture as a precondition for shame-producing awareness. Relationship is the context within which corrective shame can work.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 operates both within existing bonds (David's king offering compassion to humiliated envoys) and across bonds (military opponents humiliating nations, God humbling the proud). The divine-abasement mode (VCG-03) is universal — God's corrective humiliation of pride crosses all covenantal boundaries. CHAR-2's scope is not covenantally limited.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — The head-covering material (1Cor 11:4-5) operates within the covenant community. Jam 2:6's dishonoring of the poor operates within the community of believers. The dishonoring of Jesus (Joh 8:49) crosses the covenant community's internal boundary. CHAR-3 appears to operate most damagingly within existing relational bonds where worth-recognition is expected and violated.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — CHAR-4 operates within community contexts (VCG-01: the shameful conduct of speech in the assembly, the shameful hair practices — all community-embedded evaluations) and within covenantal contexts (the idolatrous shameful-objects of Jer 3:24; 11:13 are specifically about Israel's covenantal infidelity). VCG-02 (disordered passions) crosses community boundaries — Rom 1:26-27 addresses a pattern of moral disorder that is cultural-historical in scope.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — The commands against despising (Rom 14:3; 14:10; 1Cor 16:11; 1Th 5:20) operate within the covenant community. The Boaz-Ruth protection (Rut 2:15, vc=38516) operates across covenantal difference: Boaz protects Ruth, an outsider, from the contempt she would normally receive. The 1Sa 25:7/15 (vc=38530/38531) protection of Nabal's shepherds operates within a social context of armed men restraining themselves. CHAR-5's scope is not covenantally limited — contempt can cross any relational boundary; what is covenantally specific is the community's obligation to protect against contempt within its own relational field.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 operates specifically within the covenant relationship between the person and God: the approach to God's altar (Psa 26:6) is a covenantal act; the divine confirmation of innocence (Gen 20:6) is a covenantal response; the incapacity for innocence (Hos 8:5) is a covenantal failure condition. CHAR-6's scope is specifically covenantal-relational: it is the inner moral condition that the covenant relationship with God requires of the person.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's relational scope shows a consistent pattern: the destructive characteristics (unjust shame, contempt, dishonour) cross covenantal boundaries freely — they can fall on anyone. The constructive characteristics (corrective shame, conscience-activated moral evaluation, innocence-enabled approach) are more covenantally specific. Exceptions: Char 2's God-abasing act crosses all covenantal boundaries (God humbles all pride); Char 5's divine reversal is explicitly extended universally (1Cor 1:28 — God choosing the world's despised). Within the covenant community, specific obligations apply: protect the vulnerable from contempt (Char 5 — Rut 2:15; 1Cor 16:11), honour the worth of all members (Char 3 — Jam 2:6), exercise corrective shame with proper moral grounding (Char 1's entrepō; Char 4). These community-internal obligations are the cluster's most directly applicable finding for relational ethics.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence shows CHAR-1 operating within both close relational bonds and across distance, with no evidence that proximity changes its essential character. Within close bonds: Deu 17:20 (vc=34231, M08-A1-VCG-01) — the king's heart lifted "above his brothers" — the relational bond is the covenant community; CHAR-1 operates as hierarchical self-elevation within that bond. 2Ch 26:16 (vc=34044, M08-A1-VCG-01): Uzziah's pride manifesting within his covenant relationship with God — the closest relational bond. Across distance: the national-pride corpus (M08-A3) evidences CHAR-1 in international contexts — Moab's pride against Israel (Isa 16:6, vc=33989, M08-A3-VCG-01), Babylon's pride as a global power (Isa 13:19, vc=33987, M08-A3-VCG-02). The characteristic operates across both registers without apparent difference in structure, though its specific relational consequences (contempt, domination) are shaped by the relational context.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence shows CHAR-2 operating both within close relational bonds and across distance. Within close bonds: Mat 24:49 (vc=55613, M08-B-VCG-03): the servant who beats "fellow servants" — within the same household/community bond. Mar 10:41 (vc=55587): the ten disciples' indignation at James and John — within the inner circle. Isa 3:5 (vc=34212, M08-B-VCG-02): "youth being insolent to the elder" — within the intergenerational community bond. Across distance: Jer 50:29 (vc=34127, M08-B-VCG-01): Babylon's defiance of the Holy One of Israel — the great power's CHAR-2 against God.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Within close relational bonds: 2Cor 7:4 (vc=33917) and 1Th 2:19 (vc=33913, M08-C-VCG-03) — Paul's boasting about his communities is deeply relational, grounded in shared history and genuine love. The VCG-02 corpus (2Cor 10–12) shows CHAR-3 operating within a strained relational bond (Paul and the Corinthians in conflict) — the examined boasting serves the relational purpose of defending apostolic integrity within an existing community relationship. Across relational distance: VCG-01 boasting of wealth or achievements is more typical of cross-distance social display.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence evidences CHAR-4 operating within close relational bonds specifically. 1Cor 4:6 (vc=33937, M08-D-VCG-01): the Corinthian community's partisan conceit within the community — existing bonds of loyalty to teachers becoming the occasion for inter-group inflation. 1Cor 5:2 (vc=33940, M08-D-VCG-01): the community's collective CHAR-4 response to an internal moral failure — within the existing bond of the community. 2Cor 12:20 (vc=33942, M08-D-VCG-02): Paul's fear of finding fusiōsis within the Corinthian community he knows personally.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The evidence evidences CHAR-5 operating primarily in the structural-power relational register, where distance from the vulnerable is itself a product of the structural elevation. Eze 16:49 (vc=33979, M08-E-VCG-01): Sodom's CHAR-5 creates the relational distance from the poor — the ease-dwelling community is structurally separated from the needy neighbour. Obd 3 (vc=65674, M08-E-VCG-02): "you who live in the clefts of the rock, in your lofty dwelling" — the physical elevation creates the relational distance from others that reinforces CHAR-5's self-sufficiency conviction.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster comparison reveals that M08 characteristics operate within close relational bonds across all five, and the damage within existing bonds is particularly evidenced for CHAR-4 (community inflation — 1Cor 4:6, M08-D-VCG-01; 1Cor 5:2, M08-D-VCG-01) and CHAR-2 (domineering authority within the servant-community — Mat 24:49, M08-B-VCG-03). CHAR-5 shows that the structural elevation creates relational distance within the same community (Sodom's ease-pride creating distance from the poor — Eze 16:49, M08-E-VCG-01). The cluster-synthesis: M08 characteristics are particularly damaging within existing relational bonds — the pride that is directed toward those one knows and lives with produces the most destructive relational consequences, because it exploits the trust and proximity of the bond.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The household register (Eph6:1; Col3:20; Pro30:17; 1Ti3:4) evidences the characteristic operating within the closest existing bonds (family). The gospel-obedience register (Act6:7; Rom1:5; 16:26) evidences it operating across the broadest possible scope (all nations). The characteristic operates in both — within close bonds and across distance — but the inner quality varies: within close bonds, the household submission is shaped by long-term formation (1Ti3:4 — cultivated household quality); across the broader gospel scope, the submission is the decisive single act of reorientation (Act6:7 — priests becoming obedient to the faith). The characteristic adapts its operational form to the relational context.

**[CHAR-3]** S — The two-verse corpus does not directly address relational-bond variation. Both verses operate in the divine-human relational register without specifying whether the human is within covenant or outside it. Psa34:18 uses generalising language ("the brokenhearted," "the crushed in spirit") without covenant-specificity; Isa57:15 similarly uses the general "him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit."

**[CHAR-4]** E — Heb5:2 operates within the established priestly covenant structure — the metriopatheō is the high priest's characteristic within his covenantally-defined mediating role. Act9:38 operates within the early Christian community network (disciples in Joppa calling for Peter in Lydda) — the responsive readiness is called for within the network of believers. Both evidences operate within established relational structures rather than across relational distance; the characteristic appears to be expressed within existing relational frameworks where the person has a defined role or relationship.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The three verses evidence the characteristic operating within established relational structures: the civic community (1Ti2:2 — under governance), the household (1Ti3:4 — within the family), and the teaching relationship (Tit2:7 — between teacher and learners). All three are existing relational bonds rather than across relational distance. The characteristic appears particularly suited to ordering established authority-relationships rather than crossing relational distance.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The evidence shows the characteristic operating primarily within established covenantal and communal structures: the Israel community at Sinai (Exo35 — within the covenant people), the pre-temple Israel community (1Ch28:21), the temple-restoration community under Hezekiah (2Ch29:31), and the individual psalmist's relationship with God (Psa51:12). The characteristic operates within existing relational structures rather than across relational distance.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence shows operation in both contexts without explicit contrast between them. The ka.na corpus operates primarily within the covenantal bond (Israel before God, Israelite kings before the covenant Lord); the horizontal humility in Phili2:3 and Eph4:2 operates within the body of believers. However, 2Ch30:11 evidences humility crossing tribal and political divisions — "men of Asher, of Manasseh, and of Zebulun" overcoming their northern-kingdom separation from Jerusalem through the inner act of humbling. This suggests the characteristic can operate across relational distance and social division. Mat11:29 — the invitation to learn humility from Jesus — crosses the distance between the divine teacher and all who are "weary and burdened," suggesting the characteristic operates beyond existing relational bonds.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics are evidenced within established relational structures rather than across relational distance. Humility (CHAR-1): primarily within covenantal bonds (Israel before God) and community bonds (believers toward one another); though 2Ch30:11 (men from Asher and Manasseh overcoming tribal-political division through humbling) and Mat11:29 (invitation extended to all who are weary) suggest the characteristic can cross relational distance. Submission (CHAR-2): both within the closest bonds (household — Eph6:1) and the broadest scope (all nations — Rom1:5; 16:26), confirming its operation in both registers. Contrition (CHAR-3): exclusively within the individual's relationship with God — the most intimate relational context possible; no evidence of operation across relational distance. Meekness and Gentleness (CHAR-4): within priestly-covenant structures (Heb5:2) and early Christian community networks (Act9:38). Dignity (CHAR-5): within civic, household, and pedagogical structures — all established relational contexts. Willing-heartedness (CHAR-6): within the covenant community (Exo35; 1Ch28:21; 2Ch29:31) and the individual's relation to God (Psa51:12). Cluster-level: M09 characteristics are evidenced within established relational structures; the evidence does not address operation across relational distance as a primary concern.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The corpus shows clear differentiation. Within existing bonds: Gen 42:22 (brothers sinning against a brother — deep family bond), 1Sa 19:4/5 (king sinning against a servant who has done only good — overlord/servant bond), Mat 18:15 (brother sinning against a brother within the community of disciples). Across bonds: Gen 40:1 (cupbearer and baker sinning against their lord — authority relationship). The evidence shows that sinning within existing bonds is treated as particularly grievous — Jonathan frames sinning against innocent David as a moral horror ("Why then will you sin against innocent blood?", 1Sa 19:5) precisely because the king-servant bond makes the sinning a betrayal. Sinning against relational partners magnifies the moral weight.

**[CHAR-10]** E — Yes. (1) *Enticement*: 2Pe 2:18 — the enticers use the teaching relationship (they are teachers with authority — "speaking loud boasts") as the delivery medium; the existing relational bond between teacher and student is the channel. Within existing relational bonds, enticement is more effective (the trust is already established). (2) *Hypocrisy*: Gal 2:13 — the collective hypocrisy operates entirely within existing relational bonds — the Jewish community at Antioch; sunupokrinomai requires pre-existing social bonds to operate. (3) *Apostasy*: Act 21:21 — the covenantal community bond (the Jewish covenantal identity) is what is being abandoned; apostasy operates by dissolving an existing relational-covenantal bond.

**[CHAR-11]** E — Yes. (1) *Within the covenant community*: Rom 3:9 — "all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin" — the condition operates without distinction within the covenant community (Jews) and outside it (Greeks); even the covenant relation does not exempt persons from the condition. Heb 5:3 — the high priest must sacrifice for his own sins alongside the people's — the condition operates within the most intimate covenant-service relationship. (2) *Across relational distance*: Luk 24:47 — "repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed to all nations" — the remedy is extended across all relational and cultural distances; the condition's universality makes the remedy's scope equally universal.

**[CHAR-12]** E — Yes. Within the community context: 1Jo 5:16 — "if anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life" — the enslaving power's grip on a sinning brother is addressed within the existing relational bond of community membership; the intercessory prayer operates through the relational bond between brother and brother. The enslaving power that holds the sinning brother can be addressed from within the relational bond. For sin leading to death (1Jo 5:16) — even the relational bond cannot provide sufficient intercessory access; the enslavement has moved beyond the relational-bond remedy.

**[CHAR-13]** E — Yes. Within existing covenantal bonds: Lev 26:18-28 — the sevenfold discipline is specifically covenant-internal; the record's consequences escalate within the established God-Israel relationship. The record's weight is heavier within the covenant precisely because the relational expectations are higher (1Ki 14:22 — Judah "provoked him to jealousy... more than all that their fathers had done"). Across relational distance: Gen 18:20 — Sodom's sin is great enough to reach God as an outcry even from outside the covenant community; the divine record operates without respect to covenantal membership.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Yes. Within the covenant community (VCG-01/03): the priestly atonement system operates within the established God-Israel covenant bond; the atonement is conducted within the Tabernacle/Temple as the designated relational space between God and Israel. Exo 30:16 — the atonement money brings Israel "to remembrance before the Lord" — the covenant relationship is the operative relational field. Yes — the data reveals that compassion operates distinctly in both modes, and the distinction is analytically important.

**Within existing relational bonds (chesed):** The chesed vocabulary is definitionally relational — it names the loyal love that sustains bonds through time and across failure. Chesed operates within the covenantal relationship: between God and Israel, between king and vassal, between person and community. Within these bonds, compassion functions as the quality that holds the bond together when it would otherwise break — it sustains rather than initiates.

**Across relational distance and difference (splanchnizō):** The Synoptic compassion-movements operate primarily across distance: toward crowds of strangers (Matt 9:36), toward a widow unknown to Jesus (Luke 7:13), toward a leper (Mark 1:41 — ritually excluded). The most explicit example is Luke 10:33: the Good Samaritan's compassion crosses the sharpest relational boundary in the data — the Jewish/Samaritan divide, a boundary of ethnic, cultural, and religious hostility. Compassion here is explicitly operating across difference rather than within existing bonds.

**Key finding:** The vocabulary differentiates these two operational modes: chesed operates within bonds; splanchnizō operates across distance and difference. These are not in competition — they name different relational registers of the same characteristic. But they are distinct enough that the programme should not conflate them.

Human-to-human love is the ethical core of the love commandment. The data shows it operating in five structural relationships: (a) **Neighbour** (H7453 rea — 173 active) — the primary OT ethical form: 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Lev 19:18); (b) **Enemy** (Mat 5:44, OBS-103-143) — the most demanding NT extension — love directed to those who actively oppose the person; (c) **Community of faith** (Joh 13:34, 1Th 3:12) — mutual love as the community's defining practice; (d) **Friendship** (filos, H0157H, dod vocabulary) — personal loyal love; (e) **Family** (filadelfia, filostorgos, filoteknos, filandros) — love within natural and spiritual family structures. The human-to-human direction is the most evidentially diverse — spanning obligation (neighbour-love), choice (friendship), natural bond (family), and cost (enemy-love).
